Lowering corporate tax rates doesn't boost long-term job growth because the primary benefit flows to shareholders and executives, not workers. Empirical studies show the largest gains go to stock buybacks, dividends, and C-suite compensation—not wages or hiring.

Business investment decisions are driven by demand, regulation, labor costs, and technology—not marginal tax rate changes. When firms already have strong cash flow (as they do in low-interest environments), additional tax savings don't translate to new employment.

The U.S. corporate tax rate fell from 35% to 21% in 2017, yet the subsequent job gains were pre-determined by economic expansion, not caused by the rate cut. Long-term growth comes from investments in infrastructure, education, and R&D—areas where government spending directly creates jobs and productivity gains.

Additionally, tax cuts create revenue shortfalls that often force reduced public investment or higher deficits—both of which can crowd out future economic activity and job creation more than any temporary private-sector gain offsets.
